Asynchronous dynamics of isomorphic Boolean networks
Florian Bridoux, Aymeric Picard Marchetto, Adrien Richard

Abstract
A Boolean network is a function f : { 0 , 1 } n → { 0 , 1 } n f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n} from which several dynamics can be derived, depending on the context. The most classical ones are the synchronous and asynchronous dynamics. Both are digraphs on { 0 , 1 } n \{0,1\}^{n} , but the synchronous dynamics (which is identified with f f ) has an arc from x x to f ⁡ ( x ) f(x) while the asynchronous dynamics 𝒜 ⁡ ( f ) \mathcal{A}(f) has an arc from x x to x + e i x+e_{i} whenever x i ≠ f i ​ ( x ) x_{i}\neq f_{i}(x) . Clearly, f f and 𝒜 ⁡ ( f ) \mathcal{A}(f) share the same information, but what can be said on these objects up to isomorphism? We prove that if 𝒜 ⁡ ( f ) \mathcal{A}(f) is only known up to isomorphism then, with high probability, f f can be fully reconstructed up to isomorphism. We then show that the converse direction is far from being true. In particular, if f f is only known up to isomorphism, very little can be said on the attractors of 𝒜 ⁡ ( f ) \mathcal{A}(f) . For instance, if f f has p p fixed points, then 𝒜 ⁡ ( f ) \mathcal{A}(f) has at least max ⁡ ( 1 , p ) \max(1,p) attractors, and we prove that this trivial lower bound is tight: there always exists h ∼ f h\sim f such that 𝒜 ⁡ ( h ) \mathcal{A}(h) has exactly max ⁡ ( 1 , p ) \max(1,p) attractors. But 𝒜 ⁡ ( f ) \mathcal{A}(f) may often have much more attractors since we prove that, with high probability, there exists h ∼ f h\sim f such that 𝒜 ⁡ ( h ) \mathcal{A}(h) has Ω ⁡ ( 2 n ) \Omega(2^{n}) attractors.



1
Introduction

A
Boolean network
with
n
components is a function

f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n},\quad x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\mapsto f(x)=(f_{1}(x),\dots,f_{n}(x)).

Many dynamics can be derived from
f
, the most two common ones being the
synchronous
and the
asynchronous
dynamics, denoted
\mathcal{S}(f)
and
\mathcal{A}(f)
, respectively. Both are digraphs with vertex set
\{0,1\}^{n}
but they differ in their arcs:
\mathcal{S}(f)
has an arc from
x
to
f(x)
for every
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
(and is usually identified with
f
), while
\mathcal{A}(f)
has an arc from
x
to
y
whenever
x
and
y
only differ in component
i
and
f_{i}(x)\neq x_{i}
. See Figure
1
for an illustration.

Figure 1:
Synchronous (left) and asynchronous (right) dynamics of the shift
f(x_{1},x_{2})=(x_{2},x_{1})
.

The choice of dynamics depends on the context. Notably, Boolean networks are very classical models for the dynamics of gene networks, introduced in the seminal papers of Kaufman
[
10
]
and Thomas
[
16
]
; but Kaufman proposed to use the synchronous dynamics while Thomas argued that the asynchronous dynamics is more realistic. Since then, both dynamics are used to model the same object, which is disturbing since the two dynamics often describe radically different behaviors. It then seems natural to compare these dynamics, see e.g.
[
14
,
5
,
4
,
6
,
7
,
11
]
.

Many important dynamical parameters are invariant by isomorphism such as the number of and size of attractors
1
1

1

The
attractors
of a digraph are its terminal strong components.
, the transient length and so on. In other words, one often consider that the important part of the behaviors described by
\mathcal{S}(f)
or
\mathcal{A}(f)
is contained in the structure of the state transitions rather than in state labels. This leads us to study the relationships between
\mathcal{S}(f)
and
\mathcal{A}(f)
up to isomorphism (the isomorphic relation is denoted
\sim
). In other words, given two Boolean networks
f,h
, we are interested in the following two questions:

•

What can be said on
h
when
\mathcal{A}(h)\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
?

•

What can be said on
\mathcal{A}(h)
when
h\sim f
?

Our first result shows that
\mathcal{A}(h)\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
almost always implies
h\sim f
: the unlabelled synchronous dynamics can almost always be fully reconstructed from the unlabelled asynchronous dynamics.

Theorem 1
.

Taking
f
uniformly at random, the probability that
\mathcal{A}(h)\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
implies
h\sim f
for every
h
tends to
1
as
n\to\infty
.

Our second result shows that, on the other direction, the unlabelled asynchronous dynamics cannot be fully reconstructed from the unlabelled synchronous dynamics, except if this latter corresponds to a constant or the identity.

Theorem 2
.

If
f\neq\mathrm{cst},\mathrm{id}
and
n\geq 3
, there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)\not\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
.

However, we may ask if at least some important parameters of the unlabelled asynchronous dynamics can be reconstructed from the unlabelled synchronous dynamics. Arguably, one of the most important parameters is the number of attractors in
\mathcal{A}(f)

[
12
,
13
,
9
,
17
]
, and we thus focus on this parameter. A basic observation is that
f(x)=x
if and only if
x
is of out-degree
0
in
\mathcal{A}(f)
. In other words, fixed points of
f
correspond to attractors of
\mathcal{A}(f)
of size one. Since
\mathcal{A}(f)
has always at least one attractor, we deduce that

\mathcal{A}(f)
has at least
\max(1,\mathrm{fp}(f))
attractors,

(1)

where
\mathrm{fp}(f)
is the number of fixed points of
f
. This is thus a lower bound on the number of asynchronous attractors that only depends on the unlabelled synchronous dynamics. But can we say something stronger? We provide a negative answer, showing that this trivial lower bound is always tight.

Theorem 3
.

If
f
has a fixed point, there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has exactly
\mathrm{fp}(f)
attractors. Otherwise, there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a unique attractor, which is of size
\leq 4
.

Even if we cannot extract a non-trivial lower bound on the number of asynchronous attractors from the unlabelled synchronous dynamics, we may ask if a non-trivial upper bound should be obtained. However, we will prove that, most often, any such upper-bound is in
\Omega(2^{n})
. Indeed, we will prove that if
f^{2}
has
d
images, then there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
\lfloor d/10\rfloor
attractors, each of size
\leq 4
(Lemma
17
). Since the expected value of
d
is asymptotically
(1-e^{-1+e^{-1}})2^{n}\simeq 0.468\cdot 2^{n}

[
3
]
, and since the limit distribution of
d
is a Gaussian distribution with variance
c\cdot 2^{n}
for some constant
c>0

[
1
]
, we obtain the following.

Theorem 4
.

Taking
f
uniformly at random, the probability that there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
0.046\cdot 2^{n}
attractors, each of size
\leq 4
, tends to
1
as
n\to\infty
.

Concerning attractor sizes, the upper bound
4
in Theorems
3
and
4
is tight, in that if
f
is a permutation without limit cycle of length
\leq 2
, then the attractors of
\mathcal{A}(f)
are all of size
\geq 4
(Remark
2
). On the opposite direction, if
f
is a permutation without fixed point (derangement), then
\mathcal{A}(f)
may contain a unique attractor spanning the
2^{n}
configurations.

Theorem 5
.

If
f
is a derangement, there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
is strongly connected.

All these results indicate that, from the unlabelled synchronous dynamics, almost nothing can be said on the number and the size of the asynchronous attractors.

The paper is organized as follows. The main definitions are introduced in Section
2
. Then, Theorems
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
and
5
are proved in Sections
3
,
4
,
5
,
6
and
7
respectively. The most technical proofs are that of Theorems
1
and
3
.

2
Definitions

In the following,
n
is always a positive integer, and
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}[n]}}=\{1,\dots,n\}
. Elements of
\{0,1\}^{n}
are called
configurations
, and those of
[n]
are called
components
. Let
x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
. The addition
x+y
is computed component-wise modulo
2
. We denote by
\mathbf{0}
(resp.
\mathbf{1}
) the configuration
x
such that
x_{i}=0
(resp.
1
) for all
i\in[n]
. We set
\bar{x}_{i}=x_{i}+1
and
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\bar{x}}}=x+\mathbf{1}
. For
i\in[n]
we denote by
e_{i}
the configuration
z
such that
z_{i}=1
and
z_{j}=0
for all
j\neq i
. More generally, given distinct
i_{1},\dots,i_{k}\in[n]
, we set
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}e_{i_{1},\dots,i_{k}}}}=e_{i_{1}}+\cdots+e_{i_{k}}
. The
weight

w(x)
of
x
is the number of
i\in[n]
with
x_{i}=1
. The
distance

d(x,y)
between
x
and
y
is the number of
i\in[n]
such that
x_{i}\neq y_{i}
. Hence,
d(x,y)=w(x+y)
. The partial order
\leq
on
\{0,1\}^{n}
is defined by
x\leq y
if and only if
x_{i}\leq y_{i}
for all
i\in[n]
. Given
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
, we set
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\bar{X}}}=\{0,1\}^{n}\setminus X
. Given
a,b\in\{0,1\}^{n}
, we denote by
(a\leftrightarrow b)
be the permutation of
\{0,1\}^{n}
that transposes
a
and
b
, that is,
(a\leftrightarrow b)(a)=b
,
(a\leftrightarrow b)(b)=a
and
(a\leftrightarrow b)(x)=x
for all
x\neq a,b
.

Given a graph (resp. digraph)
G
, we denote by
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}V(G)}}
its vertex set and
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}E(G)}}
its edges (resp. arcs). If
G
is undirected and has an edge between
u
and
v
we write
uv\in E(G)
or
vu\in E(G)
indifferently. If
G
is directed and has an edge from
u
to
v
we write
uv\in E(G)
or
u\to v\in E(G)
. Given two digraphs
G,V
, we write
G\,{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\sim}}\,H
to mean that that
G
and
H
are isomorphic, that is, there exits a bijection
\pi:V(G)\to V(H)
such that, for all
u,v\in V(G)
, we have
uv\in E(G)
if and only if
\pi(u)\pi(v)\in E(H)
; then
\pi
is an isomorphism from
G
to
H
. We denote by
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}C_{\ell}}}
the (unlabelled) directed cycle of length
\ell
, and
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}P_{\ell}}}
the (unlabelled) directed path of length
\ell
(with
\ell+1
vertices). Given an (unlabelled) digraph
G
and
k\geq 1
, we denote by
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}kG}}
the (unlabelled) digraph which consists of
k
vertex-disjoint copies of
G
. Given (unlabelled) digraphs
G
and
H
, the disjoint union of
G
and
H
is denoted
G+H
. Given
U\subseteq V(G)
, we denote by
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}G[U]}}
the subgraph of
G
induced by
U
.

We denote by
F(n)
the set of functions
f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to\{0,1\}^{n}
. Let
f\in F(n)
. The
synchronous graph
of
f
is the directed graph
\mathcal{S}(f)
on
\{0,1\}^{n}
with an arc from
x
to
f(x)
for all
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
. A
limit cycle
of
f
is a cycle of
\mathcal{S}(f)
. A
periodic configuration
of
f
of period
p
is a configuration that belongs to a cycle of
\mathcal{S}(f)
of length
p
. A
fixed point
of
f
is a configuration
x
such that
f(x)=x
. Equivalently, it is a periodic configuration of period
1
. We denote by
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathrm{FP}(f)}}
the set of fixed points of
f
and
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathrm{fp}(f)}}=|\mathrm{FP}(f)|
. The
asynchronous graph
of
f\in F(n)
is the digraph
\mathcal{A}(f)
on
\{0,1\}^{n}
with an arc from
x
to
x+e_{i}
for all
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
and
i\in[n]
with
f_{i}(x)\neq x_{i}
. An
attractor
of
\mathcal{A}(f)
is an inclusion-minimal non-empty set
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
\mathcal{A}(f)
has no arc from
X
to
\bar{X}
. Given two functions
f,h\in F(n)
, we write
f\sim h
to means that
f
and
h
are isomorphic, that is,
\mathcal{S}(f)\sim\mathcal{S}(h)
.

3
Synchronous reconstruction

In this section, we prove Theorem
1
, that for almost all Boolean networks
f
, if
\mathcal{A}(h)\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
then
h\sim f
: the unlabelled synchronous dynamics can be fully reconstructed from the unlabelled asynchronous dynamics.

First, remark that this is not true for
all
Boolean networks as shown in Figure
2
. In this example, where
n=3
, the asynchronous dynamics only contains
3
arcs among the
n2^{n}=24
possible arcs, and is thus very sparse. Usual asynchronous dynamics are not sparse: they contain
n2^{n-1}
arcs in average. We will prove that isomorphisms between such usual asynchronous dynamics preserve the distance between configurations, which allows the reconstruction of the synchronous dynamics without possible ambiguity (up to isomorphism).

\mathcal{A}(f)&&\mathcal{A}(h)\end{array}

Figure 2:
Example of non-isomorphic Boolean networks with isomorphic asynchronous graphs.

To proceed to the details, we need some definitions. Let
Q_{n}
denotes the
n
-cube
, that is, the graph on
\{0,1\}^{n}
where two configurations
x,y
are adjacent iff
d(x,y)=1
. An
isometry
is an automorphism of
Q_{n}
, that is, a permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
\pi(x)\pi(y)\in E(Q_{n})
for all
xy\in E(Q_{n})
. We say that two graphs or digraphs
G,H
on
\{0,1\}^{n}
are
isometric
if there exists an isomorphism between
G
and
H
which is an isometry.

Lemma 1
.

Let
f,h\in F(n)
and suppose that
\mathcal{A}(f)
and
\mathcal{A}(h)
are isometric. Then
f\sim h
.

Proof.

Given
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
, let
\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)
be the out-neighbors of
x
in
\mathcal{A}(f)
. For all
i\in[n]
, we have
f_{i}(x)\neq x_{i}
iff
\mathcal{A}(f)
has an arc from
x
to
x+e_{i}
. Hence,

\displaystyle f(x)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle x+\sum_{x+e_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)}e_{i}

(2)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle x+\sum_{y\in\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)}(x+y).

(3)

Suppose that some isomorphism
\pi
from
\mathcal{A}(f)
to
\mathcal{A}(h)
is an isometry. Then, there exists a permutation
\sigma
of
[n]
and a configuration
a\in\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
\pi(x)=\sigma(x)+a
for all
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
, where
\sigma(x)=(x_{\sigma(1)},\dots,x_{\sigma(n)})
; see
[
8
,
15
,
2
]
for instance. Given
x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
, we have
\sigma(x+y)=\sigma(x)+\sigma(y)
. Thus,
\pi(x+y)=\sigma(x+y)+a=\sigma(x)+\sigma(y)+a=\pi(x)+a+\pi(y)+a+a=\pi(x)+\pi(y)+a
. We deduce that, for every odd integer
k
and
x^{1},\dots,x^{k}\in\{0,1\}^{n}
, we have
\pi(x^{1}+\dots+x^{k})=\pi(x^{1})+\dots+\pi(x^{k})
. Since (
3
) is a sum of
2|\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)|+1
terms (in which the term
x
appears
|\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)|+1
times), and since
y\in\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)
iff
\pi(y)\in\mathcal{A}_{h}(\pi(x))
(because
\pi
is an isomorphism from
\mathcal{A}(f)
to
\mathcal{A}(h)
), we have

\pi(f(x))=\pi(x)+\sum_{y\in\mathcal{A}_{f}(x)}(\pi(x)+\pi(y))=\pi(x)+\sum_{\pi(y)\in\mathcal{A}_{h}(\pi(x))}(\pi(x)+\pi(y))=h(\pi(x)).

Thus,
\pi
is an isomorphism from
f
to
h
.
∎

The above lemma allows us to translate Theorem
1
into a problem concerning spanning subgraphs of
Q_{n}
(that is, subgraphs of
Q_{n}
obtained by deleting edges only). So let
\Omega_{n}
be the set of spanning subgraphs of
Q_{n}
and
G\in\Omega_{n}
. An
embedding
of
G
is a permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
\pi(x)\pi(y)\in E(Q_{n})
for all
xy\in E(G)
. An edge
xy\in E(Q_{n})
is
solid
in
G
if
\pi(x)\pi(y)\in E(Q_{n})
for all embedding
\pi
of
G
. We denote by
\tilde{G}
the graph obtained from
G
by adding all the edges of
Q_{n}
that are solid in
G
. Clearly, every edge of
G
is solid, that is,
G\subseteq\tilde{G}
. We say that
G
is
solid
if
\tilde{G}=Q_{n}
; equivalently, all the embedding of
G
are isometries.

Let
U\mathcal{A}(f)
be the undirected version of
\mathcal{A}(f)
that is, the graph in
\Omega_{n}
with an edge between
x
and
y
if and only if
\mathcal{A}(f)
has an arc from
x
to
y
or from
y
to
x
. Our interest for solid spanning subgraphs of
Q_{n}
comes from the following property, which is an easy consequence of Lemma
1
. It shows that if
U\mathcal{A}(f)
is solid, then the unlabelled synchronous dynamics of
f
can be reconstructed from its unlabelled asynchronous dynamics.

Lemma 2
.

For every
f,h\in F(n)
, if
U\mathcal{A}(f)
is solid then

\mathcal{A}(f)\sim\mathcal{A}(h)~\Longrightarrow~f\sim h.

Proof.

Let
\pi
be an isomorphism from
\mathcal{A}(f)
to
\mathcal{A}(h)
. Then,
\pi
is an isomorphism from
U\mathcal{A}(f)
to
U\mathcal{A}(h)
, and thus
\pi
is an embedding of
U\mathcal{A}(f)
. Since
U\mathcal{A}(f)
is solid,
\pi
is an isometry. So
\mathcal{A}(f)
and
\mathcal{A}(h)
are isometric and thus
f\sim h
by Lemma
1
.
∎

Consequently, to prove Theorem
1
it is sufficient to prove that, taking
f\in F(n)
uniformly at random, the probability that
U\mathcal{A}(f)
is solid tends to
1
as
n\to\infty
. Given
xy\in E(Q_{n})
and
f\in F(n)
taken uniformly at random, the probability that
\mathcal{A}(f)
has no arc from
x
to
y

and
no arc from
y
to
x
is
1/4
. Hence, for all
xy\in E(Q_{n})
, the probability that
xy
is an edge of
U\mathcal{A}(f)
is
3/4
and these events are pairwise independent. Hence, to prove Theorem
1
it is sufficient to prove that if
G
is a random spanning subgraph of
Q_{n}
obtained by selecting each edge of
Q_{n}
with probability
p=3/4
then the probability that
G
is solid (
\tilde{G}=Q_{n}
) tends to
1
as
n\to\infty
. We will actually prove something slightly stronger, Theorem
6
below, that
p\geq 0.72
is enough for this property.

Let us first fix some notations. If
A\subseteq E(Q_{n})
and
G\in\Omega_{n}
, we abusively write
A\subseteq G
instead of
A\subseteq E(G)
, and we denote by
|G|
the number of edges in
G
(thus
|Q_{n}|=n2^{n-1}
). Given an underlying fixed probability
0\leq p\leq 1
of edge selection in
Q_{n}
, we denote by
\mathrm{Pr}
the probability function over the sample space
\Omega_{n}
where the probability of an outcome
H\in\Omega_{n}
is

\mathrm{Pr}[G=H]=p^{|H|}(1-p)^{|Q_{n}|-|H|}.

Theorem 6
.

For
0.72\leq p\leq 1
we have

\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{Pr}[\tilde{G}=Q_{n}]=1.

We begin with a simple observation.

Lemma 3
.

For every
G,H\in\Omega_{n}
, if
G\subseteq H
then
\tilde{G}\subseteq\tilde{H}
.

Proof.

Let
xy\in E(\tilde{G})
and let
\pi
be an embedding of
H
. Since
G\subseteq H
,
\pi
is also an embedding of
G
, and since
xy
is solid in
G
, we have
\pi(x)\pi(y)\in E(Q_{n})
, and thus
xy\in E(\tilde{H})
.
∎

For
A,B\subseteq E(Q_{n})
, it is rather intuitive that
\mathrm{Pr}[B\subseteq G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}]\geq\mathrm{Pr}[B\subseteq G]
: the fact that a set
A
of edges is solid in
G
only increases the probability that a set
B
of edges is contained in
G
.
It is equivalently intuitive that
\mathrm{Pr}[B\not\subseteq G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}]\leq\mathrm{Pr}[B\not\subseteq G]
as the event
B\not\subseteq G
is simply the negation of the event
B\subseteq G
. We prove this below in a stronger form.

Lemma 4
.

Let
A\subseteq E(Q_{n})
and disjoint sets
B_{1},\dots,B_{k}\subseteq E(Q_{n})
. Let
P
be the set of
G\in\Omega_{n}
with
B_{i}\not\subseteq G
for all
1\leq i\leq k
, and suppose that
A\subseteq\tilde{G}
for some
G\in P
. Then,

\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}]\leq\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P].

Proof.

Let
P_{0}=\Omega_{n}
and, for all
1\leq i\leq k
, let
P_{i}
be the set of
G\in\Omega_{n}
with
B_{j}\not\subseteq G
for
1\leq j\leq i
. We have,

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\not\subseteq G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}\land G\in P_{i-1}]

(4)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{k}1-\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\subseteq G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}\land G\in P_{i-1}].

Fix
1\leq i\leq k
and let us prove, by induction on
|B_{i}|
, that

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\subseteq G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}\land G\in P_{i-1}]\geq\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\subseteq G].

(5)

For
|B_{i}|=0
this is obvious so suppose that
|B_{i}|>0
. Let
e\in B_{i}
and
X:=B_{i}\setminus e
. Let also

\displaystyle p_{X}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[X\subseteq G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}\land G\in P_{i-1}],

\displaystyle p_{e}

\displaystyle:=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[e\in G\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}\land G\in P_{i-1}\land X\subseteq G].

Hence, (
5
) says

p_{X}\cdot p_{e}\geq\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\subseteq G]=\mathrm{Pr}[X\subseteq G]\cdot\mathrm{Pr}[e\in G].

By induction,
p_{X}\geq\mathrm{Pr}[X\subseteq G]
thus it is sufficient to prove that
p_{e}\geq\mathrm{Pr}[e\in G]=p
. Let
R
be the set of
H\in P_{i-1}
such that
A\subseteq\tilde{H}
and
X\subseteq H
. Let
R_{0}
be the set of
H\in R
with
e\not\in H
and
R_{1}:=R\setminus R_{0}
. Hence,

p_{e}=\mathrm{Pr}[G\in R_{1}\mid G\in R].

If
R_{0}
is empty, then
R=R_{1}
thus
p_{e}=1
and we are done. So suppose that
R_{0}
is not empty. For every
H\in R_{0}
, let
H^{\prime}
be obtained from
H
by adding
e
. We have
X\subseteq H\subseteq H^{\prime}
and thus
A\subseteq\tilde{H}\subseteq\tilde{H}^{\prime}
by Lemma
3
. Furthermore, if
i=1
then
H^{\prime}\in P_{i-1}
and otherwise, since
e\not\in B_{j}
for
1\leq j\leq i-1
, we have
H^{\prime}\in P_{i-1}
. Thus,
H^{\prime}\in R_{1}
. Hence,
H\mapsto H^{\prime}
is an injection from
R_{0}
to
R_{1}
. For every
H\in R_{0}
,

\mathrm{Pr}[G=H]=p^{|H|}(1-p)^{|Q_{n}|-|H|}=\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)p^{|H^{\prime}|}(1-p)^{|Q_{n}|-|H^{\prime}|}=\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)\mathrm{Pr}[G=H^{\prime}].

Hence, since
H\mapsto H^{\prime}
is an injection from
R_{0}
to
R_{1}
,

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[G\in R_{0}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{H\in R_{0}}\mathrm{Pr}[G=H]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)\sum_{H\in R_{0}}\mathrm{Pr}[G=H^{\prime}]

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)\sum_{F\in R_{1}}\mathrm{Pr}[G=F]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)\mathrm{Pr}[G\in R_{1}].

Consequently, setting
r_{0}:=\mathrm{Pr}[G\in R_{0}]
and
r_{1}:=\mathrm{Pr}[G\in R_{1}]
, we have

p_{e}=\mathrm{Pr}[G\in R_{1}\mid G\in R]=\frac{r_{1}}{r_{0}+r_{1}}\geq\frac{r_{1}}{\left(\frac{1-p}{p}\right)r_{1}+r_{1}}=p.

This proves (
5
). Plugging (
5
) into (
4
) we obtain

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P\mid A\subseteq\tilde{G}]

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{k}1-\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\subseteq G]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{Pr}[B_{i}\not\subseteq G]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P].

∎

The fact that an edge is solid in
G
is somewhat evanescent. This leads us to find a concrete sufficient condition for an edge to be solid. We need some definitions. A
staple

S
on an edge
xy
of
Q_{n}
is a path of
Q_{n}
of length
3
between
x
and
y
, that is, three edges in
Q_{n}
of the form
\{xx^{\prime},x^{\prime}y^{\prime},y^{\prime}y\}
. Hence, there are
n-1
staples on
xy
, and they are pairwise disjoint; see Figure
3
. The crucial observation is that if
G
contains at least
4
staples on
xy
, then
xy
is solid. Actually, the weaker condition that
\tilde{G}
contains at least
4
staples on
xy
is still sufficient for
xy
to be solid:

0000
1000
0100
0010
0001
1100
1010
1001

Figure 3:
The three staples on
\mathbf{0}e_{1}
for
n=4
.

Lemma 5
.

Let
G\in\Omega_{n}
and
xy\in E(Q_{n})
. If
\tilde{G}
contains at least
4
staples on
xy
then
xy\in E(\tilde{G})
.

Proof.

Let
\pi
be an embedding of
G
. Suppose that
\tilde{G}
contains
4
distinct staples on
xy
, say
S_{1},\dots,S_{4}
, and let
S_{i}=\{xx^{i},x^{i}y^{i},y^{i}y\}
. Then,
P_{i}:=\pi(x)
-
\pi(x^{i})
-
\pi(y^{i})
-
\pi(y)
is a path of length
3
in
Q_{n}
between
\pi(x)
and
\pi(y)
, and thus
d(\pi(x),\pi(y))\leq 3
and
d(\pi(x),\pi(y))
is odd. If
d(\pi(x),\pi(y))=3
then
Q_{n}
has exactly
3
edges-disjoint paths of length
3
between
\pi(x)
and
\pi(y)
, which is a contradiction since
P_{1},P_{2},P_{3},P_{4}
are edges-disjoint paths of length
3
between
\pi(x)
and
\pi(y)
. Thus,
d(\pi(x),\pi(y))<3
and this forces
d(\pi(x),\pi(y))=1
. Consequently,
xy\in\tilde{G}
.
∎

We are now in position to prove Theorem
6
.

Proof of Theorem
6
.

If
p=1
the result is obvious so suppose that
0.72\leq p<1
. Let
x^{1}y^{1},\dots,x^{m}y^{m}
be an enumeration of the
m=n2^{n-1}
edges of
Q_{n}
in such a way that for all
1\leq i\leq j\leq m
we have
w(x^{i})<w(y^{i})
and
w(x^{i})\leq w(x^{j})
. Let
A_{0}=\emptyset
and, for
1\leq i\leq m
, let
A_{i}
be the set of edges
x^{j}y^{j}
with
1\leq j\leq i
. We have

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[\tilde{G}=Q_{n}]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{Pr}[x^{i}y^{i}\in\tilde{G}\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}]

(6)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{m}1-\mathrm{Pr}[x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}].

Let

q=1-p^{3}+0.01,\qquad\ell=\frac{1-p}{1-p^{3}},

and note that
q<1
since
p\geq 0.72
. In order to lower bound the probability that
\tilde{G}=Q_{n}
, we will give an upper bound on the probability that
x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}
under the condition
A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}
, which only depends on
w(x^{i})
: for
n
large enough,

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}]\leq q^{n}\ell^{w(x^{i})}.

(7)

Let
\mathcal{S}^{+}
be the set of staples
\{x^{i}x,xy,yy^{i}\}
on
x^{i}y^{i}
with
w(x^{i})<w(x)
, and
\mathcal{S}^{-}
be the set of staples
\{x^{i}x,xy,yy^{i}\}
on
x^{i}y^{i}
with
w(x)<w(x^{i})
. We have
|\mathcal{S}^{+}|=n-w(x^{i})-1
and
|\mathcal{S}^{-}|=w(x^{i})
. Given a staple
S=\{x^{i}x,xy,yy^{i}\}
, we set
S^{\prime}=\{yy^{i}\}
if
S\in\mathcal{S}^{-}
and
S^{\prime}=S
otherwise. The crucial observation is that if
S\in\mathcal{S}^{-}
then
x^{i}x,xy\in A_{i-1}
so

\displaystyle A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\left(S\subseteq\tilde{G}\iff S^{\prime}\subseteq\tilde{G}\quad\forall S\in\mathcal{S}^{+}\cup\mathcal{S}^{-}\right).

(8)

Given
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{+}\cup\mathcal{S}^{-}
, let
P(\mathcal{B})
be the set of
G\in\Omega_{n}
such that
S^{\prime}\not\subseteq G
for all
S\in\mathcal{B}
. For
S\in\mathcal{B}
, the probability that
S^{\prime}\subseteq G
is
p^{3}
if
S\in\mathcal{S}^{+}
and
p
otherwise, so

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P(\cal B)]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(1-p^{3})^{|\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{S}^{+}|}(1-p)^{|\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{S}^{-}|}.

By Lemma
5
, if
x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}
then
\tilde{G}
contains at most
3
staples on
x^{i}y^{i}
. Equivalently, there exists a set
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{+}\cup\mathcal{S}^{-}
of size at least
n-4
such that
S\not\subseteq\tilde{G}
for all
S\in\mathcal{B}
; by (
8
), under the condition
A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}
, this is equivalent to
\tilde{G}\in P(\mathcal{B})
, which implies
G\in P(\mathcal{B})
. Consequently, denoting by
\Lambda
the set of
\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{S}^{+}\cup\mathcal{S}^{-}
of size at least
n-4
, we deduce, using the union bound for the first inequality and Lemma
4
for the second, that

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}]

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\sum_{\mathcal{B}\in\Lambda}\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P(\mathcal{B})\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}]

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle\sum_{\mathcal{B}\in\Lambda}\mathrm{Pr}[G\in P(\mathcal{B})]

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{\mathcal{B}\in\Lambda}(1-p^{3})^{|\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{S}^{+}|}(1-p)^{|\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{S}^{-}|}.

Since
|\mathcal{B}|\geq n-4
we have
|\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{S}^{+}|\geq n-w(x^{i})-4
and
|\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{S}^{-}|\geq w(x^{i})-3
. Furthermore,
|\Lambda|=\sum_{k=0}^{3}{n-1\choose n-1-k}\leq n^{3}
. We deduce that

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}]

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle n^{3}(1-p^{3})^{n-w(x^{i})-4}(1-p)^{w(x^{i})-3}.

Since
1-p^{3}<q
, for
n
large enough we have
n^{3}(1-p^{3})^{n-4}(1-p)^{-3}\leq q^{n}
and thus

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[x^{i}y^{i}\not\in\tilde{G}\mid A_{i-1}\subseteq\tilde{G}]

\displaystyle\leq

\displaystyle q^{n}(1-p^{3})^{-w(x^{i})}(1-p)^{w(x^{i})}~=~q^{n}\ell^{w(x^{i})}.

This proves (
7
).

Pulgging (
7
) in (
6
) and noting that, for any integer
0\leq w\leq n-1
there are
(n-w){n\choose w}
edges
x^{i}y^{i}
with
w(x^{i})=w
, we obtain, using the rough bound
(n-w){n\choose w}\leq n(en/w)^{w}
,

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[\tilde{G}=Q_{n}]

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{m}1-q^{n}\ell^{w(x^{i})}

(9)

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\prod_{w=0}^{n-1}\left(1-q^{n}\ell^{w}\right)^{(n-w){n\choose w}}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle(1-q^{n})^{n}\prod_{w=1}^{n-1}\left(1-q^{n}\ell^{w}\right)^{n(en/w)^{w}}.

Since
1-x\geq e^{-2x}
for any
0\leq x\leq 1/2
, and since
0\leq q^{n}\ell^{w}\leq q^{n}\leq 1/2
for
n
large enough, we have
1-q^{n}\ell^{w}\geq e^{-2q^{n}\ell^{w}}
and
1-q^{n}\geq e^{-2q^{n}}
. Combining this with (
9
) we obtain

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[\tilde{G}=Q_{n}]

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle e^{-2nq^{n}}\prod_{w=1}^{n-1}e^{-2q^{n}\ell^{w}n(en/w)^{w}}.

The derivative of the real function
x\mapsto\ell^{x}(en/x)^{x}
is
x\mapsto(e\ell n/x)^{x}\ln(\ell n/x)
. Hence, this derivative has a unique root, namely
\ell n
, and is positive for
x<\ell n
and negative for
x>\ell n
. Consequently, the maximum of
\ell^{x}(en/x)^{x}
is obtained for
x=\ell n
. We deduce that

\displaystyle\mathrm{Pr}[\tilde{G}=Q_{n}]

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle e^{-2nq^{n}}\prod_{w=1}^{n-1}e^{-2q^{n}\ell^{\ell n}n(en/{\ell n})^{\ell n}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle e^{-2nq^{n}}\prod_{w=1}^{n-1}e^{-2n(qe^{\ell})^{n}}

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle e^{-2[n^{2}(qe^{\ell})^{n}+nq^{n}]}.

Since
p\geq 0.72
we have
qe^{\ell}<1
. Hence,
n^{2}(qe^{\ell})^{n}+nq^{n}
tends to
0
as
n\to\infty
and thus

\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{Pr}[\tilde{G}=Q_{n}]=1.

∎

4
Asynchronous reconstruction

In this section, we prove Theorem
2
, that if
f
is neither constant nor the identity and
n\geq 3
, then there exists
h\sim f
with
\mathcal{A}(h)\not\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
: the unlabelled asynchronous dynamics cannot be fully reconstructed from the unlabelled synchronous dynamics.

For every
f\in F(n)
, we denote by
\Delta^{+}(f)
the set of configurations
x
such that
f(x)=\bar{x}
; equivalently,
\Delta^{+}(f)
is the set of configurations with out-degree
n
in
\mathcal{A}(f)
. Similarly, let
\Delta^{-}(f)
be the set of configurations with in-degree
n
in
\mathcal{A}(f)
. We say that
f
contains
2P_{1}
if its synchronous graph contains two vertex-disjoint paths of length
1
; equivalently, there exist configurations
x,y
such that
x,y,f(x),f(y)
are all distinct. The next lemma shows that the presence of
2P_{1}
is sufficient for the existence of
h\sim f
such that
|\Delta^{+}(h)|\neq|\Delta^{+}(f)|
, which implies
\mathcal{A}(h)\not\sim\mathcal{A}(f)
.

Lemma 6
.

If
f\in F(n)
contains
2P_{1}
, then there exists
h\sim f
with
|\Delta^{+}(h)|\neq|\Delta^{+}(f)|
.

Proof.

Suppose that
f
contains
2P_{1}
. Hence, there are configurations
a,b
such that
a,b,f(a),f(b)
are all distinct. Let
x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
with
0<d(x,y)<n
(so
x,y,\bar{x}
and
\bar{y}
are all distinct). Let

\pi=(a\leftrightarrow x)\circ(b\leftrightarrow y)\circ(f(a)\leftrightarrow\bar{x})\circ(f(b)\leftrightarrow\bar{y})

and

h^{1}=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1},\quad h^{2}=(y\leftrightarrow\bar{x})\circ h^{1}\circ(y\leftrightarrow\bar{x}),\quad h^{3}=(\bar{x}\leftrightarrow\bar{y})\circ h^{1}\circ(\bar{x}\leftrightarrow\bar{y}).

See Figure
4
for an illustration.

For all
i\in[3]
, let
\Delta^{i}=\Delta^{+}(h^{i})
. We will prove that either
|\Delta^{2}|<|\Delta^{1}|
or
|\Delta^{3}|<|\Delta^{1}|
, which proves the lemma (because
f\sim h^{1}\sim h^{2}\sim h^{3}
). Let
X=\{x,y,\bar{x},\bar{y}\}
and
Y=\{0,1\}^{n}\setminus X
. For all
i,j\in[3]
, if
z\in\Delta^{i}\cap Y
then
h^{i}(z)=\bar{z}\in Y
thus
h^{i}(z)=h^{j}(z)
since
(y\leftrightarrow\bar{x})
and
(\bar{x}\leftrightarrow\bar{y})
act as the identity on
Y
, so that
z\in\Delta^{j}\cap Y
. Consequently,
\Delta^{i}\cap Y\subseteq\Delta^{j}\cap Y
and thus

\Delta^{1}\cap Y=\Delta^{2}\cap Y=\Delta^{3}\cap Y.

Hence, to prove that
|\Delta^{2}|<|\Delta^{1}|
or
|\Delta^{3}|<|\Delta^{1}|
, we have to prove that
|\Delta^{2}\cap X|<|\Delta^{1}\cap X|
or
|\Delta^{3}\cap X|<|\Delta^{1}\cap X|
. Since
|\Delta^{1}\cap X|\geq 2
(because
h^{1}(x)=\bar{x}
and
h^{1}(y)=\bar{y}
), it is actually sufficient to prove that
|\Delta^{2}\cap X|\leq 1
or
|\Delta^{3}\cap X|=0
. Suppose first that
h^{1}(\bar{x})\neq\bar{y}
or
h^{1}(\bar{y})\neq\bar{x}
. Then
h^{2}(y)\neq\bar{y}
or
h^{2}(\bar{y})\neq y
, and since
h^{2}(x)=y\neq\bar{x},h^{2}(\bar{x})=\bar{y}\neq x
we have
|\Delta^{2}\cap X|\leq 1
. Suppose now that
h^{1}(\bar{x})=\bar{y}
and
h^{1}(\bar{y})=\bar{x}
. Then,
h^{3}(\bar{x})=\bar{y}\neq x
and
h^{3}(\bar{y})=\bar{x}\neq y
, and since
h^{3}(x)=\bar{y}\neq\bar{x},h^{3}(y)=\bar{x}\neq\bar{y}
we have
|\Delta^{3}\cap X|=0
.
∎

Figure 4:

Illustration for Lemma
6
.

We now give another sufficient condition for the existence of
h\sim f
with
|\Delta^{+}(h)|\neq|\Delta^{+}(f)|
.

Lemma 7
.

Let
f\in F(n)
with
f\neq\mathrm{id}
and
n\geq 3
. If
f
does not contain
2P_{1}
and has at least
2
periodic configurations, then there exists
h\sim f
with
|\Delta^{+}(h)|\neq|\Delta^{+}(f)|
.

Proof.

Suppose that
f
satisfies the conditions of the statement. Since
f\neq\mathrm{id}
, there exists a configuration
a
such that
a\neq f(a)
and such that
f(a)
is a periodic configuration; if
f
has a limit cycle of length at least
2
, we chose
a
in this limit cycle so that both
a
and
f(a)
are periodic configurations. Let
g=(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow f(a))\circ f\circ(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow f(a))
. Then,
g(a)=\bar{a}
and
|\Delta^{+}(g)|\geq 1
. We prove below that there exists
h\sim g
with
|\Delta^{+}(h)|<|\Delta^{+}(g)|
, which implies the lemma.

Suppose first that all the periodic configurations of
g
are fixed points (thus,
a
is a non-periodic configuration). Let
X
be the non-periodic configurations of
g
distinct from
a
. Then,
\bar{a}
is a fixed point of
g
and since
g
does not contain
2P_{1}
, either
g(X)=\{a\}
or
g(X)=\{\bar{a}\}
. Furthermore, since
g
has at least two periodic configurations, it has a fixed point
b\neq\bar{a}
. We then consider two cases, illustrated in Figure
5
.

1.

First, suppose that
g(X)=\{a\}
(see Figure
5
-1). Let
h=(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow b)\circ g\circ(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow b)
. If
x\neq h(x)
and
x\neq a
then
h(x)=a
and
x\neq\bar{a}
(since
\bar{a}
is a fixed point of
h
). Since
h(a)=b\neq\bar{a}
this proves that
|\Delta^{+}(h)|=0
.

2.

Second, suppose that
g(X)=\{\bar{a}\}
(see Figure
5
-2). Let
h=(a\leftrightarrow b)\circ g\circ(a\leftrightarrow b)
. If
x\neq h(x)
then
h(x)=\bar{a}
and
x\neq a
(since
a
is a fixed point of
h
). Thus,
|\Delta^{+}(h)|=0
.

Suppose now that
g
has a limit cycle
L
of length
2
. Since we chose
a
so that both
a
and
f(a)
are periodic configurations of
f
, we have that
a
and
g(a)=\bar{a}
are periodic configurations of
g
, so the configurations of
L
are
a
and
\bar{a}
, which implies
|\Delta^{+}(g)|\geq 2
(see Figure
5
-3). Furthermore, since
g
does not contain
2P_{1}
, all the periodic configurations
x\neq a,\bar{a}
are fixed points. Let
X
be the set of non-periodic configurations of
g
. Since
g
does not contain
2P_{1}
, either
g(X)=\{a\}
or
g(X)=\{\bar{a}\}
. The two cases being symmetric, we assume, without loss, that
g(X)=\{a\}
. Let
b\neq a,\bar{a}
and
h=(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow b)\circ g\circ(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow b)
. Since
h(a)=b
and
h(b)=a
, we have
a,b\not\in\Delta^{+}(h)
. If
x\neq h(x)
and
x\neq a,b
then
h(x)=a
, and thus
x\in\Delta^{+}(h)
if and only if
x=\bar{a}
. We deduce that
\Delta^{+}(h)
is either empty or only contains
\bar{a}
. Hence,
|\Delta^{+}(h)|\leq 1<|\Delta^{+}(g)|
.

Suppose finally that
g
has a limit cycle
L
of length
\ell\geq 3
. Since
g
does not contain
2P_{1}
, we have
\ell=3
and all the configurations outside of
L
are fixed points, so
g
is a permutation and
L
contains
a,\bar{a}
and a third configuration
b
(see Figure
5
-4). Let
c
be a fixed point of
g
distinct from
\bar{b}
, which exists since
n\geq 3
, and let
h=(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow c)\circ g\circ(\bar{a}\leftrightarrow c)
. We have
h(a)=c\neq\bar{a}
,
h(c)=b\neq\bar{c}
and
h(b)=a\neq\bar{b}
. Furthermore,
h(x)=x\neq\bar{x}
for all
x\neq a,b,c
, and thus,
|\Delta^{+}(h)|=0
.
∎

Figure 5:
Illustration for Lemma
7
.

By the two previous lemmas, it remains to treat the case where
f
does not contain
2P_{1}
and has a unique periodic configuration. We prove below that these properties forces
|\Delta^{+}(f)|=1
. However, if
f
is not constant there exists
h\sim f
with
|\Delta^{-}(h)|\neq|\Delta^{-}(f)|
. This finishes the proof of Theorem
2
.

Lemma 8
.

Let
f\in F(n)
with
f\neq\mathrm{cst}
and
n\geq 3
. If
f
does not contain
2P_{1}
and has a unique periodic configuration, then
|\Delta^{+}(f)|=1
and there exists
h\sim f
with
|\Delta^{-}(h)|\neq|\Delta^{-}(f)|
.

Proof.

Suppose that
f
does not contain
2P_{1}
. Let
b
be the unique periodic configuration of
f
, which is thus a fixed point, and let
a
be a pre-image of
b
. Since
f\neq\mathrm{cst}
and
f
does not contain
2P_{1}
, for all
x\neq a,b
we have
f(x)=a
. We then easily check that
\Delta^{+}(f)=\{a\}
if
b=\bar{a}
and
\Delta^{+}(f)=\{\bar{a}\}
otherwise.

Let
\pi_{1},\pi_{2}
be permutations of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
\pi_{1}
sends
a,b
on
\mathbf{0},\mathbf{1}
, and
\pi_{2}
sends
a,b
on
\mathbf{0},e_{1,2}
. Let
h^{1}=\pi_{1}\circ f\circ\pi_{1}^{-1}
and
h^{2}=\pi_{2}\circ f\circ\pi_{2}^{-1}
. See Figure
6
for an illustration. We will prove that

\Delta^{-}(h^{1})=\{\mathbf{0},e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{n}\},\qquad\Delta^{-}(h^{2})=\{\mathbf{0}\}.

and thus
|\Delta^{-}(h^{1})|\neq|\Delta^{-}(h^{2})|
, which implies the lemma. Let
k\in\{1,2\}
and
i\in[n]
. Since
h^{k}(e_{i})=\mathbf{0}
,
\mathcal{A}(h^{k})
has an arc from
e_{i}
to
\mathbf{0}
, and thus
\mathbf{0}\in\Delta^{-}(h^{k})
. Let
x
with
w(x)\geq 2
. Then, there exists
j\in[n]
such that
x_{j}=1
and
x+e_{j}\neq e_{1,2}
. Then,
h^{k}(x+e_{j})=\mathbf{0}
and thus
\mathcal{A}(h^{k})
has no arc from
x+e_{j}
to
x
, so that
x\not\in\Delta^{-}(h^{k})
. Hence, so far,
\mathbf{0}\in\Delta^{-}(h^{k})\subseteq\{\mathbf{0},e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\}
. Since
h^{1}(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{1}
,
\mathcal{A}(h^{1})
has an arc from
\mathbf{0}
to
e_{i}
. Furthermore, for
j\neq i
we have
e_{i,j}\neq\mathbf{1}
(since
n\geq 3
) so
h^{1}(e_{i,j})=\mathbf{0}
and we deduce that
\mathcal{A}(h^{1})
has an arc from
e_{i,j}
to
e_{i}
. Hence,
e_{i}\in\Delta^{-}(h^{1})
and this proves
\Delta^{-}(h^{1})=\{\mathbf{0},e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{n}\}
. Finally, since
h^{2}(\mathbf{0})=e_{1,2}
,
\mathcal{A}(h^{2})
has no arc from
\mathbf{0}
to
\{e_{3},\dots,e_{n}\}
and since
h^{2}(e_{1,2})=e_{1,2}
,
\mathcal{A}(h^{2})
has no arc from
e_{1,2}
to
\{e_{1},e_{2}\}
. Thus,
\Delta^{-}(h^{2})=\{\mathbf{0}\}
.
∎

5
Few and small attractors

5.1
Asynchronous convergence toward fixed points

In this subsection we prove the first assertion in Theorem
3
: if
f
has at least one fixed point, there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has
\mathrm{fp}(f)
attractors. Since
\mathrm{fp}(f)=\mathrm{fp}(h)
, this is equivalent to say that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a path from any configuration to a fixed point of
h
. We actually prove something stronger; the precise statement, Theorem
7
below, needs some definitions. An arc from
x
to
y
in
\mathcal{A}(f)
is
increasing
if
x<y
and
decreasing
otherwise. A path is
decreasing
if all its arcs are decreasing. Hence, a decreasing path from
x
to
y
is of length
d(x,y)\leq n
. A path is
almost decreasing
if all its arc, except possibly one, are decreasing. Hence, an almost-decreasing path from
x
to
y
is of length at most
d(x,y)+1\leq n+1
.

Theorem 7
.

Let
f\in F(n)
with at least one fixed point. There exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration to
\mathrm{FP}(h)
.

To illustrate the proof technic, suppose that
f
has a unique fixed point, say
z
, and no other periodic configurations, that is
f
is a nilpotent function. Then
\mathcal{S}(f)
is an in-tree plus a loop on the root
z
. Let
\preceq
be a topological order of this is in-tree, that is, a total order on
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
f(x)\prec x
for all
x\neq z
. There is then a permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
x\preceq y
implies
w(\pi(x))\leq w(\pi(y))
, we say that such a permutation is monotone. Since
z
is the
\preceq
-minimal element, we have
\pi(z)=\mathbf{0}
by monotonicity, and thus
\mathbf{0}
is the unique fixed point of
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
. Furthermore, for every
x\neq\mathbf{0}
, we have
\pi^{-1}(x)\neq z
, thus
f(\pi^{-1}(x))\prec\pi^{-1}(x)
so that
w(h(x))\leq w(x)
by monotonicity. Since
x
is not a fixed point of
h
, we deduce that
h_{i}(x)<x_{i}
for some
i\in[n]
, that is,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing arc starting from
x
. It follows that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\mathbf{0}
. See Figure
8
for an illustration.

Figure 8:
(a) Unlabelled synchronous dynamics of a nilpotent function
f\in F(3)
with a topological order, increasing from left to right. (b) Function
h\sim f
obtained with a monotone permutation. (c) Decreasing transitions of
\mathcal{A}(h)
, showing that there is a decreasing path from any configuration to
000
.

With a similar but more technical argument, we can obtain a more general result of convergence by decreasing paths, Lemma
9
below. The statement is kept as general as possible, in order to be used later to treat the case where
f
has no fixed point, and it involves the several definitions.

Let
f,h\in F(n)
and
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
. We say that
h
is
X
-converging (by decreasing paths)
if
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
X\cup\mathrm{FP}(h)
. We say that
h
is
robustly
X
-converging
if
\pi\circ h\circ\pi^{-1}
is
X
-converging for every permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
acting as the identity on
\bar{X}
. Taking
\pi=\mathrm{id}
, we see that if
h
is robustly
X
-converging, then
h
is
X
-converging. We write
h\sim_{X}f
to means that
h\sim f
and that, for all
x\in X
,

•

h(x)=f(x)
if
f(x)\in X
;

•

h(x)\not\in X
otherwise.

In other words,
h\sim_{X}f
iff and only if
h\sim f
and the subgraph of
\mathcal{S}(h)
induced by
X
is equal to the subgraph of
\mathcal{S}(f)
induced by
X
. Finally, we say that
X
is an
down set
if
x\in X
and
y\leq x
implies
y\in X
; and
X
is an
upper set
if
\bar{X}
is a down set.

Lemma 9
.

Let
f\in F(n)
and let
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
be a non-empty down set with
f(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. Suppose that, for all
1<\ell<n
,
\bar{X}
contains at least
{n-1\choose\ell-1}+1
configurations of weight
\ell
. There exists a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}f
.

This lemma will be proved later (in Section
5.3
); for the moment we show that it easily implies Theorem
7
.

Proof of Theorem
7
(assuming Lemma
9
).

We consider two cases.

1.

Suppose that
f
is not a permutation. Since
f
has a fixed point, there exists
g\sim f
such that
g(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}
. Let
X=\{\mathbf{0}\}
, which is a down set. Since
g
is not a permutation, we have
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. Furthermore, for all
1<\ell<n
, the number of
x\in\bar{X}
with
w(x)=\ell
is
{n\choose\ell}>{n-1\choose\ell-1}
. Thus, by Lemma
9
, there exists a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}g
. Hence,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\{\mathbf{0}\}\cup\mathrm{FP}(h)
. Since
h\sim_{X}g
we have
h(\mathbf{0})=g(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}
and thus
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\mathrm{FP}(h)
.

2.

Suppose that
f
is a permutation. If
f=\mathrm{id}
the result is obvious so suppose that
f\neq\mathrm{id}
. Since
f
has a fixed point and
f\neq\mathrm{id}
, there exists
g\sim f
such that
g(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}
and
g_{1}(e_{1})=0
. Let
X=\{\mathbf{0},e_{1}\}
, which is a down set. Since
g(e_{1})\neq e_{1}
and
g(e_{1})\neq\mathbf{0}=g(\mathbf{0})
(because
g
is a permutation), we have
g(e_{1})\in\bar{X}
and thus
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. Furthermore, for all
1<\ell<n
, the number of
x\in\bar{X}
with
w(x)=\ell
is
{n\choose\ell}>{n-1\choose\ell-1}
.
Thus, by Lemma
9
, there exists a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}g
. Hence,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\{\mathbf{0},e_{1}\}\cup\mathrm{FP}(h)
, and since
h\sim_{X}g
we have
h(\mathbf{0})=g(\mathbf{0})=\mathbf{0}
. We then consider two subcases:

2.1.

Suppose that
h_{1}(e_{1})=0
. Then
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing arc from
e_{1}
to
\mathbf{0}
. Thus,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\mathrm{FP}(h)
.

2.2.

Suppose that
h_{1}(e_{1})=1
. Then
h(e_{1})\not\in X
: since
h\sim_{X}g
, if
g(e_{1})\in X
then
h_{1}(e_{1})=g_{1}(e_{1})=0
, a contradiction; so
g(e_{1})\not\in X
and thus
h(e_{1})\not\in X
. Let
\pi=(\mathbf{0}\leftrightarrow e_{1})
and
h^{\prime}=\pi\circ h\circ\pi
. Since
h
is robustly
X
-converging and
\pi
acts as the identity on
\bar{X}
,
h^{\prime}
is
X
-converging:
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\{\mathbf{0},e_{1}\}\cup\mathrm{FP}(h^{\prime})
. Furthermore,
h^{\prime}(e_{1})=\pi(h(\pi(e_{1})))=\pi(h(\mathbf{0}))=\pi(\mathbf{0})=e_{1}
and
h^{\prime}(\mathbf{0})=\pi(h(\pi(\mathbf{0})))=\pi(h(e_{1}))=h(e_{1})
, where the last equality holds since
h(e_{1})\not\in X
. So
h^{\prime}_{1}(\mathbf{0})=h_{1}(e_{1})=1
. Thus,
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has an increasing arc from
\mathbf{0}
to
e_{1}
and we deduce that
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration to
\mathrm{FP}(h^{\prime})
.

∎

5.2
Asynchronous convergence toward a unique small attractor

In this subsection we prove the second assertion of Theorem
3
for
n\geq 5
, with additional information on the paths reaching the unique small asynchronous attractors; the case
n\leq 4
is treated in Appendix
A
.

Theorem 8
.

Let
f\in F(n)
without fixed point,
n\geq 5
. There exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an attractor
A
of size
\leq 4
and
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration to
A
.

The proof technic follows that of Theorem
7
. To explain the analogy, let us first give a rough summary of the proof of Theorem
7
. First, we obtain
g\sim f
by “plugging” in
X
a “pattern”, which is either a fixed point
\mathbf{0}
(case 1) or a fixed point
\mathbf{0}
and
e_{1}
with
g_{1}(e_{1})=0
(case 2); the choice is done so that
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
and
\mathcal{A}(g)
has a decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to a fixed point. We then use Lemma
9
to obtain a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}g
. If
\mathcal{A}(h)
still has a decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to a fixed point then we are done (case 1 and 2.1). Otherwise, we apply a “correction”: we swap configurations in
X
to obtain
h^{\prime}\sim h
so that
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to a fixed point (case 2.2). Since
h
is robustly
X
-converging,
h^{\prime}
is still
X
-converging and we are done.

To prove Theorem
8
we proceed similarly, except that we obtain
g\sim f
by “plugging” in
X
more sophisticated “patterns”. Any such pattern forces
\mathcal{A}(g)
to contain an attractor
A\subseteq X
of size at most
4
and an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to
A
. Furthermore, the pattern is chosen so that
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. We then use Lemma
9
to obtain a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}g
. Then
A
is still an attractor of
\mathcal{A}(h)
, and if
\mathcal{A}(h)
still has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to
A
then we are done. Otherwise, we apply a “correction”: we permute configurations in
X
to obtain
h^{\prime}\sim h
so that
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to an attractor
A^{\prime}
with the same size as
A
. Since
h
is robustly
X
-converging,
h^{\prime}
is still
X
-converging and we are done. Actually, this works well except if
f^{2}=\mathrm{id}
, and for that case we have a direct proof (Lemma
13
).

There are 16 possibles patterns: patterns
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}_{1}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}_{2}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}_{3}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}_{4}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}_{5}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}_{6}}}
are described in Figure
9
and called
closed patterns
; for
a=0,1
, patterns
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}^{a}_{1}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}^{a}_{2}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}^{a}_{3}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}^{a}_{4}}},{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{P}^{a}_{5}}}
are described in Figures
10
and
11
and called
a
-open patterns
. A closed pattern
\mathcal{P}_{k}
is a digraph with vertices in
\{0,1\}^{n}
, and we say that
f

contains

\mathcal{P}_{k}
if
\mathcal{P}_{k}
is a subgraph of
\mathcal{S}(f)
. An
a
-open pattern
\mathcal{P}^{a}_{k}
is a digraph with vertices in
\{0,1\}^{n}
plus a
special arc
, which is
x\to a*
for some configuration
x
. We then say that
x
is the
special configuration
of the pattern and that
\mathcal{S}(f)

contains

x\to a*
if
f_{1}(x)=a
. Then
f

contains
a pattern
\mathcal{P}^{a}_{k}
if
\mathcal{S}(f)
contains every arc of
\mathcal{P}^{a}_{k}
, including the special arc.

Each pattern
\mathcal{P}
is associated with an
asynchronous pattern

{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{P})}}
, described in Figures
9
,
10
and
11
; we easily check that if
f
contains
\mathcal{P}
then
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{P})
is a subgraph of
\mathcal{A}(f)
. This asynchronous pattern
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{P})
has a unique attractor, denoted
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}A(\mathcal{P})}}
, which is of size at most
4
(represented in blue in Figures
9
,
10
and
11
). The vertex set of
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{P})
(which does not include the configurations
a*
of the
a
-open patterns) is denoted
X(\mathcal{P})
and
{\it{\color[rgb]{0.68,0,0}\bar{X}(\mathcal{P})}}
is its complement. Note that
\mathcal{A}(\mathcal{P})
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X(\mathcal{P})
to
A(\mathcal{P})
. Note also that
X(\mathcal{P})
is a down set.

1
-open patterns.

The following is straightforward to check, and show that patterns produce small attractors.

Lemma 10
.

If
f\in F(n)
contains a pattern
\mathcal{P}
then
A(\mathcal{P})
is an attractor of
\mathcal{A}(f)
of size
\leq 4
and
\mathcal{A}(f)
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X(\mathcal{P})
to
A(\mathcal{P})
.

We say that
f

properly contains
a pattern
\mathcal{P}
if
f
contains
\mathcal{P}
and
X=X(\mathcal{P})
satisfies the condition of Lemma
9
; since
X
is always a down set, this condition is:
f(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
and, for all
1<\ell<n
,
\bar{X}
contains at least
{n-1\choose\ell-1}+1
configurations of weight
\ell
. We now show that patterns are unavoidable (this corresponds to the first step in the sketch of the proof of Theorem
8
given above):

Lemma 11
.

Let
f\in F(n)
without fixed point, and suppose that
f^{2}\neq\mathrm{id}
and
n\geq 5
. There exists
g\sim f
such that
g
properly contains a closed or
0
-open pattern
\mathcal{P}
.

Proof.

Let
\mathcal{P}
be any pattern and
X=X(\mathcal{P})
. Firstly, for
4\leq\ell<n
, since
X
contains no configuration of weight
\ell
,
\bar{X}
contains
{n\choose\ell}>{n-1\choose\ell-1}
configurations of weight
\ell
. Secondly, since
X
contains at most one configuration of weight
3
,
\bar{X}
contains least
{n\choose 3}-1
configurations of weight
3
; this exceeds
{n-1\choose 2}
since
n\geq 5
. Thirdly, since
X
contains at most three configurations of weight
2
,
\bar{X}
contains at least
{n\choose 2}-3
configurations of weight
2
; this exceeds
{n-1\choose 1}
since
n\geq 5
. Consequently,
g
properly contains
\mathcal{P}
iff
g
contains
\mathcal{P}
and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. So we only have to prove that there exists
g\sim f
such that
g
contains a closed or
0
-open pattern
\mathcal{P}
with
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
, where
\bar{X}
always means
\bar{X}(\mathcal{P})
. We proceed case by case, denoting
\ell
and
L
the minimum and maximum length of a limit cycle of
f
:

•

\ell=2
. If
L\geq 3
then, considering a cycle of length
2
and a path of length
3
in the cycle of length
L
, we deduce that there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{1}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since the image (
0*
) of the special configuration (
e_{1}
) is in
\bar{X}
. If
L=2
then
f
is not a permutation since otherwise
f^{2}=\mathrm{id}
. Furthermore, there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{1}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since
g
is not a permutation.

•

\ell=3
. If
L\geq 4
then, considering a cycle of length
3
and a path of length
4
in the cycle of length
L
, we deduce that there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{2}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since the image of the special configuration is in
\bar{X}
. If
L=3
then
f
is not a permutation, and we have two cases. If
f
has at least two limit cycles, then there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{4}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since
g
is not a permutation. If
f
has a unique limit cycle then, since
f
is not a permutation, there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{3}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since all the periodic configurations of
g
are in
X
.

•

\ell=4
. If
f
has at least two limit cycles then, considering a cycle of length
4
and a path of length
4
in a second cycle, we deduce that there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{3}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since the image of the special configuration is in
\bar{X}
. If
f
has a unique limit cycle then
f
is not a permutation. Furthermore, there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{2}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since
g
is not a permutation.

•

\ell=5
. If
f
has at least two limit cycles then, considering a cycle of length
5
and a path of length
4
in a second cycle, we deduce that there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{4}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since the image of the special configuration is in
\bar{X}
. If
f
has a unique limit cycle then
f
is not a permutation. We deduce that there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}_{5}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since all the periodic configurations of
g
are in
X
.

•

\ell=6
and
L=6
. Then
f
is not a permutation. Furthermore, there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}_{6}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since
g
is not a permutation.

•

\ell\geq 6
and
L\geq 7
. Considering a path of length
6
in a cycle of length
L
, we deduce that there exists
g\sim f
containing
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{5}
, and
g(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
since the image of the special configuration is in
\bar{X}
.

∎

The proof Theorem
8
is now an easy consequence Lemma
11
and the following lemma, which is proved assuming Lemma
9
.

Lemma 12
.

Let
g\in F(n)
without fixed point. Suppose that
g
properly contains an open or
0
-pattern
\mathcal{P}
. There exists
h\sim g
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an attractor
A
of size
\leq 4
and an almost decreasing path from any configuration to
A
.

Proof of Lemma
12
(assuming Lemma
9
).

Let
X=X(\mathcal{P})
. Since
g
properly contains
\mathcal{P}
, by Lemma
9
, there exists a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}g
. If
h
contains
\mathcal{P}
then, by Lemma
10
,
A(\mathcal{P})
is an attractor of
\mathcal{A}(h)
of size
\leq 4
and
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to
A(\mathcal{P})
, so we are done.

So suppose that
h
does not contain
\mathcal{P}
. Since
g
contains
\mathcal{P}
and
h\sim_{X}g
, we deduce that
\mathcal{P}
is a
0
-open pattern, say
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{k}
, and that
\mathcal{S}(h)
contains all the arcs of
\mathcal{P}
except its special arc
x\to 0*
, that is:
\mathcal{S}(h)
contains the induced subgraph
\mathcal{P}[X]
but
h_{1}(x)=1\neq g_{1}(x)
; since
x\in X
and
h(x)\neq g(x)
, we have
h(x)\not\in X
. Let
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}=\mathcal{P}^{1}_{k}
. Since
\mathcal{P}[X]
and
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}[X]
are isomorphic, there exists a permutation
\pi
, acting as the identity on
\bar{X}
, such that
h^{\prime}=\pi\circ h\circ\pi^{-1}
contains
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}[X]
. Since
x
is the unique vertex of out-degree zero in
\mathcal{P}[X]
,
\pi(x)
is the unique vertex of out-degree zero in
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}[X]
, that is,
\pi(x)
is the special configuration of
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
. Since
x\in X
and
h(x)\not\in X
, we have
h^{\prime}(\pi(x))=h(x)
, thus
h^{\prime}_{1}(\pi(x))=h_{1}(x)=1
and thus
\mathcal{S}(h^{\prime})
contains the special arc
\pi(x)\to 1*
of
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
. Hence,
h^{\prime}
contains
\mathcal{P}^{\prime}
(see Figure
12
for an illustration). Since
h
is robustly
X
-converging and
\pi
acts as the identity on
\bar{X}
, the function
h^{\prime}
is
X
-converging:
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
X
. By Lemma
10
,
A(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
is an attractor of
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
of size
\leq 4
and
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration in
X
to
A(\mathcal{P}^{\prime})
, so we are done.
∎

Figure 12:
Correction step in the proof of Theorem
8
for
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{P}^{0}_{1}
.

It remains to treat the case
f^{2}=\mathrm{id}
, which is easy.

Lemma 13
.

Let
f\in F(n)
with no fixed point and
f^{2}=\mathrm{id}
. There exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an attractor
A
of size
\leq 4
and an almost decreasing path from any configuration to
A
.

Proof.

Since
f
has no fixed point and
f^{2}=\mathrm{id}
,
\mathcal{S}(f)
consists of exactly
2^{n-2}
cycles of length
2
. For
n=2
, we consider the negation
h
, that is
h(x)=\bar{x}
for all
x\in\{0,1\}^{2}
; then
h\sim f
and
\mathcal{A}(h)
is strongly connected so we are done. So suppose that
n\geq 3
. Let
X=\{0,1\}^{n}\setminus\{\mathbf{0},e_{1},e_{2},\bar{e_{1}},\bar{e_{2}},\mathbf{1}\}
and let
h\in F(n)
defined by:

\begin{array}[]{lll}h(\mathbf{0})&=&e_{1}\\
h(e_{1})&=&\mathbf{0}\end{array}\quad\begin{array}[]{lll}h(\mathbf{1})&=&e_{2}\\
h(e_{2})&=&\mathbf{1}\end{array}\quad\begin{array}[]{lll}h(\bar{e_{1}})&=&\bar{e_{2}}\\
h(\bar{e_{2}})&=&\bar{e_{1}}\end{array}\quad h(x)=\bar{x}\textrm{ for all }x\in X.

One easily check that
\mathcal{S}(h)
consists of
2^{n-2}
cycles of length
2
, so
h\sim f
, and that
\{\mathbf{0},e_{1}\}
is an attractor of
\mathcal{A}(h)
. If
x\not\in\{\mathbf{0},e_{2}\}
, then there exists
i\in[n]
with
h_{i}(x)<x_{i}
and thus
\mathcal{A}(h)
has the decreasing arc
x\to x+e_{i}
. We deduce
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing path from any configuration to
\{\mathbf{0},e_{2}\}
. Since
\mathcal{A}(h)
has the almost decreasing path
e_{2}\to e_{2,3}\to e_{3}\to\mathbf{0}
,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an almost decreasing path from any configuration to
\mathbf{0}
.
∎

5.3
Decreasing Lemma

In this subsection, we prove Lemma
9
, used several times above. Let us first give a rough description of the proof. Let
f\in F(n)
and let
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
be a down set with
f(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. First we consider a total order
\preceq
on
\bar{X}
, called good order, which is a kind of topological sort of the subgraph of
\mathcal{S}(f)
induced by
\bar{X}
. Roughly, each cycle correspond to an interval, and
\preceq
is a topological sort on the acyclic part; see Figure
13
(a). The important point is that the cycles are not intertwined, and that the maximal element is in the acyclic part (the acyclic part is non-empty because
f(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
). We then consider a permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
, acting as the identity on
X
, such that
x\preceq y
implies
w(\pi(x))\leq w(\pi(y))
; such a permutation is said monotone. Setting
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
, and taking
x\in\bar{X}
with
h(x)\prec x
, we have
w(h(x))\leq w(x)
by monotonicity, and thus
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing arc starting from
x
. Also, if
f(x)\in X
then there is decreasing transition starting from
x
since
X
is a down set. Actually, if
x
is not a fixed point and there is no decreasing arc starting from
x
, that is
x<f(x)
, then
x\prec f(x)
and thus
x
is in a cycle; see Figure
13
(b). We can however fix this problem by swapping
h(x)
and a configuration
y\in\bar{X}
with the same weight; for that we need enough elements in
\bar{X}
, so the counting condition in the statement of Lemma
9
. This swap keeps the monotonicity and adds a decreasing transition starting from
x
; see Figure
13
(b). Since cycles are not intertwined, with several such corrections, we eventually obtain a permutation
\pi
, acting as the identity on
X
, such that
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
is
X
-converging; and because
X
is a down set and
\pi
acts as the identity on
X
,
h
is robustly
X
-converging and
h\sim_{X}f
.

Figure 13:

(a) Down set
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{4}
and function
f\in F(4)
represented with a good order on
\bar{X}
, from left to right. (b) Function
h\sim f
obtained with a monotone permutation: configurations in
\bar{X}
have non-decreasing weight.
h
is not
X
-converging: there is no decreasing transition starting from
0001
since
0001<h(0001)=1001
. (c) Function
h^{\prime}\sim h
obtained by swapping
1001
and
1010
.
h^{\prime}
is
X
-converging since there is no configurations
x\in\bar{X}
with
x<h^{\prime}(x)
. (d) Subgraph of
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
, showing that
h^{\prime}
is
X
-converging.

We now proceed to the details. Let
f\in F(n)
and
Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
. A
good order
of
f
on
Y
is a total order
\preceq
on
Y
such that

x\prec y\preceq f(x)~\Rightarrow~f(y)\prec y.

Lemma 14
.

Let
f\in F(n)
and
Y\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
. Then,
f
has a good order on
Y
and, for every
x\in Y\setminus f(Y)
,
f
has a good order on
Y
whose maximal element is
x
.

Proof.

Let
S_{1},\dots,S_{r}
be the connected components of the subgraph of
\mathcal{S}(f)
induced by
Y
. For
1\leq i\leq r
, let
T_{i}
be defined as follows. If
S_{i}
is acyclic then
T_{i}=S_{i}
. Otherwise,
S_{i}
has a unique cycle; we take any
x
in this cycle and let
T_{i}
be obtained from
S_{i}
by deleting the arc from
x
to
f(x)
. In both cases,
T_{i}
is a tree with a unique vertex of out-degree zero, denoted
x^{i}
. Hence,
T_{i}
has a topological order
\preceq_{i}
, that is, a total order on the vertex set of
T_{i}
with
f(x)\prec_{i}x
for all
x
in
T_{i}
distinct from
x^{i}
. Let
\preceq
be the total order on
Y
defined as follows: for all
x,y\in Y
, let
1\leq i,j\leq r
such that
x
is in
T_{i}
and
y
in
T_{j}
; then
x\preceq y
if and only if either
i<j
or
i=j
and
x\preceq_{i}y
. Then
\preceq
is a good order of
f
on
Y
. Indeed, suppose that
x\prec y\preceq f(x)
. Since
x
and
f(x)
are in the same component, say
S_{i}
, we have
x\prec_{i}f(x)
thus
x=x^{i}
. Let
S_{j}
be the connected component containing
y
. Since
x\prec y\preceq f(x)
we have
i\leq j\leq i
. Thus,
y
and
f(y)
are in
S_{i}
and since
y\neq x=x^{i}
we have
f(y)\prec_{i}y
and thus
f(y)\prec y
. Furthermore, given
x\in Y\setminus f(Y)
we can re-order the connected components so that
x
is in
S_{r}
. Since
x
has in-degree zero in
T_{r}
, we can choose
\preceq_{r}
so that
x
is its maximal element. Then
x
is the maximal element of
\preceq
.
∎

We need another lemma, giving a sufficient condition to obtain the conclusion of Lemma
9
.

Lemma 15
.

Let
f\in F(n)
and
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
be a non-empty down set. Suppose that there exists a permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
, acting as the identity on
X
, such that
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
is
X
-converging. Then
h
is robustly
X
-converging and
h\sim_{X}f
.

Proof.

The fact that
h\sim_{X}f
simply follows from the fact that
\pi
acts as the identity on
X
. So it remains to prove that
h
is robustly
X
-converging. Let
\sigma
be any permutation of
\{0,1\}^{n}
acting as the identity on
\bar{X}
, and let
h^{\prime}=\sigma\circ h\circ\sigma^{-1}
. We have to prove that
h^{\prime}
is
X
-converging, which is equivalent to prove that
\mathcal{A}(h^{\prime})
has a decreasing arc starting from each configuration in
\bar{X}\setminus\mathrm{FP}(h^{\prime})
. Suppose, for a contradiction, that there exists
x\in\bar{X}\setminus\mathrm{FP}(h^{\prime})
with
x<h^{\prime}(x)
. Since
x\in\bar{X}
and since
\bar{X}
is an upper set, we have
h^{\prime}(x)\in\bar{X}
. Since
\sigma
acts as the identity on
\bar{X}
we obtain
h(x)=h^{\prime}(x)
. Thus,
x<h(x)
, and this contradicts the fact that
h
is
X
-converging. So
h^{\prime}
is
X
-converging, and thus
h
is robustly
X
-converging.
∎

We are now ready to prove Lemma
9
, that we restate.

Lemma 9
.

Let
f\in F(n)
and let
X\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}
be a non-empty down set with
f(\bar{X})\neq\bar{X}
. Suppose that, for all
1<\ell<n
,
\bar{X}
contains at least
{n-1\choose\ell-1}+1
configurations of weight
\ell
. There exists a robustly
X
-converging function
h\sim_{X}f
.

Proof.

Let
Y=\bar{X}
which is an upper set since
X
is a down set. Since
f(Y)\neq Y
, there exists
a\in Y\setminus f(Y)
. By Lemma
14
, there exists a good order
\preceq
of
f
on
Y
whose maximal element is
a
. Given a permutation
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
, we denote by
\preceq_{\pi}
the total order on
\pi(Y)
defined as follows: for all
x,y\in Y
,

\pi(x)\preceq_{\pi}\pi(y)~\iff~x\preceq y.

Let
\Pi
be the set of permutations
\pi
of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that
\pi
acts as the identity on
X
and
\preceq_{\pi}
is
monotone
, that is

x\preceq_{\pi}y~\Rightarrow~w(x)\leq w(y).

It is obvious that
\Pi\neq\emptyset
. Furthermore, for all
\pi\in\Pi
we have
\pi(Y)=Y
(since
\pi
acts as the identity on
X
), so
\preceq_{\pi}
is a monotone total order on
Y
. In addition,
\preceq_{\pi}
is a good order of
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
. Indeed, let
x,y\in Y
and suppose that
\pi(x)\prec_{\pi}\pi(y)\preceq_{\pi}h(\pi(x))
, which is equivalent to
x\prec y\preceq f(x)
. Since
\preceq
is a good order of
f
, we have
f(y)\prec y
, and thus
h(\pi(y))=\pi(f(y))\prec_{\pi}\pi(y)
.

Given
\pi\in\Pi
, we set
f^{\pi}=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
and

Z_{\pi}=\{x\in Y\mid x<f^{\pi}(x)\}.

Suppose that there exists
\pi\in\Pi
such that
Z_{\pi}=\emptyset
, and let
h=f^{\pi}
. Since
Z_{\pi}=\emptyset
, for all
x\in Y
, we have
x\not<h(x)
thus either
h(x)=x
or
h_{i}(x)<x_{i}
for some
i\in[n]
, that is,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a decreasing arc starting from
x
. Thus,
h
is
X
-converging. By Lemma
15
,
h
is robustly
X
-converging and
h\sim_{X}f
so the lemma holds.

Consequently, it is sufficient to prove that
Z_{\pi}=\emptyset
for some
\pi\in\Pi
. Suppose, by contradiction, that
Z_{\pi}\neq\emptyset
for all
\pi\in\Pi
. Given
\pi\in\Pi
, we set

w_{\pi}=\min_{x\in Z_{\pi}}w(x).

Let
\pi\in\Pi
which maximizes
w_{\pi}
and
h=f^{\pi}
. Let
x\in Z_{\pi}
with
w(x)=w_{\pi}
. Since
x<h(x)
and
Y
is an upper set, we have
h(x)\in Y
. Since
a
is the maximal element of
\preceq
, and since
\mathbf{1}
is the maximal element of
\preceq_{\pi}
, we have
\pi(a)=\mathbf{1}
. Thus if
h(x)=\mathbf{1}
we have

a=\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{1})=\pi^{-1}(h(x))=\pi^{-1}(\pi(f(\pi^{-1}(x))))=f(\pi^{-1}(x)),

and since
x\in Y
, we have
\pi^{-1}(x)\in Y
so
a\in f(Y)
and this contradicts our choice of
a
. Consequently,
h(x)<\mathbf{1}
. Furthermore, since
|Y|<2^{n}
(because
X
is non-empty) and since
Y
is an upper set, we have
\mathbf{0}\not\in Y
. Thus,

\mathbf{0}<x<h(x)<\mathbf{1}.

Let us prove that there exists
y\in Y
such that
w(y)=w(h(x))
and
x\not\leq y
. Let
k=w(x)
and
\ell=w(h(x))
. By the above inequality, we have
1<\ell<n
. Let
A
be the set of
y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
with
w(y)=\ell
, and let
B
be the set of
y\in A
such that
x\leq y
. We have
|B|={n-k\choose\ell-k}
. By hypothesis,
|Y\cap A|>{n-1\choose\ell-1}\geq|B|
. Thus, there indeed exists
y\in(Y\cap A)\setminus B
such that
w(y)=w(h(x))
and
x\not\leq y
.

Let
\sigma=(h(x)\leftrightarrow y)
. Since
y,h(x)\in Y
,
\sigma
acts as the identity on
X
. Furthermore, it preserves the weight, and thus
\sigma\circ\pi\in\Pi
. Note that
\sigma=\sigma^{-1}
and thus
f^{\sigma\circ\pi}=\sigma\circ h\circ\sigma
.

We will prove that
w_{\sigma\circ\pi}>w_{\pi}
, which is the desired contradiction. First, we have
x\not\in Z_{\sigma\circ\pi}
since
x\not\leq y
and

f^{\sigma\circ\pi}(x)=\sigma(h(\sigma(x)))=\sigma(h(x))=y.

Let any
z\in Z_{\sigma\circ\pi}
; so
z\neq x
. Suppose, by contradiction, that
w(z)\leq w(x)
. Then
w(z)<w(y)=w(h(x))
, thus
\sigma(z)=z
and
f^{\sigma\circ\pi}(z)=\sigma(h(z))
. Since
\sigma
preserves the weight and since
z<f^{\sigma\circ\pi}(z)
we have
w(z)<w(h(z))
. Since
w(z)\leq w(x)<w(h(x))
and
z\neq x
we obtain, by monotonicity,

z\prec_{\pi}h(z),\quad z\prec_{\pi}h(x),\quad x\prec_{\pi}h(x).

Since
\preceq_{\pi}
is a good order for
h
, we cannot have
x\prec_{\pi}z\prec_{\pi}h(x)
and this forces
z\prec_{\pi}x
. Similarly, we cannot have
z\prec_{\pi}x\prec_{\pi}h(z)
and this forces
h(z)\preceq_{\pi}x
. Thus, since
\preceq_{\pi}
is monotone,

w(z)<w(h(z))\leq w(x).

Consequently,
f^{\sigma\circ\pi}(z)=\sigma(h(z))=h(z)
. Thus,
z<h(z)
, but then
z\in Z_{\pi}
and since
w(z)<w(x)
this contradicts the choice of
x
. Thus,
w(z)>w(x)
for all
z\in Z_{\sigma\circ\pi}
. But then
w_{\sigma\circ\pi}>w_{\pi}
, which is the desired contradiction.
∎

6
Many small attractors

In this section we prove Theorem
4
, that taking
f\in F(n)
uniformly at random, the probability that there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
0.046\cdot 2^{n}
attractors, each of size
\leq 4
, tends to
1
as
n\to\infty
. We start by showing that if the synchronous dynamics has many limit cycles of length
\leq 2
and many vertex-disjoint paths of length
2
, then the asynchronous dynamics can have many small attractors.

Lemma 16
.

Let
f\in F(n)
and suppose that there exists a collection of
d\leq 2^{n-3}
vertex-disjoint subgraphs of
\mathcal{S}(f)
, each isomorphic to
C_{1}
,
C_{2}
, or
2P_{2}
. There exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
d
attractors, each of size
\leq 4
.

Proof.

Let
A\subseteq\mathrm{FP}(f)
and let
B
be a set of periodic points of
f
of period
2
with
f(B)\cap B=\emptyset
. Let
P^{1},\dots,P^{2c}
be vertex-disjoint paths of length
2
contained in
\mathcal{S}(f)\setminus(A\cup B\cup f(B))
, and let
x^{k},y^{k},z^{k}
be the vertices of
P^{k}
in order. Let
d=|A|+|B|+c
and suppose that
d\leq 2^{n-3}
. We have to prove that there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
d
attractors.

Since
d\leq 2^{n-3}
there is an injection
\phi
from
A\cup B\cup[c]
to the set of configurations
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
with
x_{1}=x_{2}=x_{3}=0
. Let
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
where
\pi
is any permutation of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that:

•

\pi(a)=\phi(a)
for all
a\in A
,

•

\pi(b)=\phi(b)
and
\pi(f(b))=\phi(b)+e_{1}
for all
b\in B
,

•

\pi(x^{k})=\phi(k)+e_{2}
,
\pi(y^{k})=\phi(k)
and
\pi(z^{k})=\phi(k)+e_{1,2}
for all
k\in[c]
,

•

\pi(x^{c+k})=\phi(k)+e_{1,3}
,
\pi(y^{c+k})=\phi(k)+e_{1}
and
\pi(z^{c+k})=\phi(k)+e_{3}
for all
k\in[c]
.

Then, for any
a\in A
,
b\in B
and
k\in[c]
,
\{\phi(a)\}
,
\{\mathbf{0},e_{1}\}+\phi(b)
and
\{\mathbf{0},e_{1},e_{2},e_{1,3}\}+\phi(k)
are attractors of
\mathcal{A}(h)
; see Figure
14
for an illustration. Thus,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
d
attractors.
∎

Figure 14:

Labelling of
2P_{2}
producing the asynchronous attractor
\{\mathbf{0},e_{1},e_{2},e_{1,3}\}
.

We now prove that if
f^{2}
has many images, then
\mathcal{S}(f)
has a large collection of vertex-disjoint subgraphs isomorphic to
C_{1}
,
C_{2}
or
2P_{2}
, and thus, by the preceding lemma, the asynchronous dynamics can have many small attractors.

Lemma 17
.

Let
f\in F(n)
and let
d
be the number of images of
f^{2}
. There exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has at least
\lfloor d/10\rfloor
attractors, each of size
\leq 4
.

Proof.

Since
\lfloor d/10\rfloor\leq 2^{n}/10\leq 2^{n-3}
, by Lemma
16
, it is sufficient to prove that there exists a collection of at least
\lfloor d/10\rfloor
vertex-disjoint subgraphs of
\mathcal{S}(f)
, each isomorphic to
C_{1}
,
C_{2}
or
2P_{2}
. Let
A
be the fixed points of
f
, let
B
be the set of periodic points of
f
of period
2
(which has even size), and let
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}=\mathcal{S}(f)\setminus(A\cup B)
. It is sufficient to prove that
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
has at least
\lfloor d/10\rfloor-|A|-|B|/2
vertex-disjoint subgraphs isomorphic to
2P_{2}
or, equivalently,
\lfloor d/5\rfloor-2|A|-|B|
vertex-disjoint paths of length
2
.

Let
X
be the image set of
f^{2}
and for each
x\in X
, let
\tilde{x}
be a pre-image of
x
by
f^{2}
. Let
X^{0}=X\setminus(A\cup B)
. Since
\mathrm{FP}(f^{2})=A\cup B
, for each
x\in X^{0}
we have
\tilde{x}\neq x
and thus
\tilde{x}\to f(\tilde{x})\to x
is a path of
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
of length
2
, denoted
P_{x}
. Given
y\in X^{0}
, the paths
P_{x}
and
P_{y}
are vertex-disjoint if and only if
y\not\in\{\tilde{x},f(\tilde{x}),x,f(x),f^{2}(x)\}
. Thus, we find a collection of vertex-disjoint paths of length
2
in
\mathcal{S}^{\prime}
by selecting
x\in X^{0}
, removing
\{\tilde{x},f(\tilde{x}),x,f(x),f^{2}(x)\}
from the set
X^{0}
, and repeating the process until the set is empty. More precisely, let us write
|X^{0}|=5k+r
where
0\leq r<5
is an integer, and, for
1\leq i\leq k
, consider a sequence
x^{1},\dots,x^{k}
of configurations in
X^{0}
, and a sequence
X^{1},\dots,X^{k}
of subsets of
X^{0}
such that, for
i=1,\dots,k
:

•

x^{i}\in X^{i-1}
,

•

X^{i}=X^{i-1}\setminus\{\tilde{x}^{i},f(\tilde{x}^{i}),x^{i},f(x^{i}),f^{2}(x^{i})\}
.

These sequences exist since
|X^{i-1}|\geq|X^{0}|-5(i-1)\geq|X^{0}|-5(k-1)=5-r\geq 1
. By the argument above, the paths
P_{x^{1}},\dots,P_{x^{k}}
are vertex-disjoint, and we are done since

k=\left\lfloor\frac{|X^{0}|}{5}\right\rfloor=\left\lfloor\frac{d-|A|-|B|}{5}\right\rfloor\geq\left\lfloor\frac{d}{5}\right\rfloor-2|A|-|B|.

∎

Taking
\phi:[N]\to[N]
uniformly at random, it is proved in
[
1
]
that the limit distribution of the number of images of
\phi^{k}
is a Gaussian distribution with mean value
(1-\tau_{k})N
, where
\tau_{0}=0
and
\tau_{k+1}=e^{-1+\tau_{k}}
(the mean was previously determined in
[
3
]
), and with variance
c_{k}\cdot N
for some explicit constant
c_{k}>0
that only depends on
k
. Hence, taking
f\in F(n)
uniformly at random, the limit distribution of the number of images of
f^{2}
is a Gaussian distribution with mean value
(1-e^{-1+e^{-1}})2^{n}\simeq 0.468\cdot 2^{n}
and variance
c_{2}\cdot 2^{n}
. Hence, for any
d<(1-e^{-1+e^{-1}})
, the probability that
f^{2}
has at least
d\cdot 2^{n}
images tends to
1
as
n\to\infty
. Combining this with Lemma
17
, we obtain Theorem
4
.

Remark 2
.

The upper bound
4
on attractors sizes in Theorems
3
and
4
is tight. Indeed, suppose that
f
is a permutation without limit cycles of length
\leq 2
. Then it is clear that all the attractors of
\mathcal{A}(f)
are of size
\geq 3
. If
\mathcal{A}(f)
has an attractors
A
of size
3
, then
A=\{x,x+e_{i},x+e_{j}\}
for some
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
and distinct
i,j\in[n]
. But then, since
A
is an attractor, we have
f(x+e_{i})=f(x+e_{j})=x
, a contradiction. Thus all the attractors of
\mathcal{A}(f)
are of size
\geq 4
.

7
One big attractor

For which
f\in F(n)
does there exist
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a large attractor? If
f
has a fixed point, then it is clear that
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an attractor of size one for every
h\sim f
. So we have to forbid fixed points. In this section, we show that this basic necessary condition is sufficient when
f
is a permutation: if
f
is a permutation without fixed point (derangement), then there exists
h\sim f
such that
\mathcal{A}(h)
is strongly connected, that is,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an attractor spanning the
2^{n}
configurations; this is Theorem
5
.

The proof is based on the existence of a particular coloring of the synchronous graph. We need some definitions. Given digraphs
G,H
, an
H
-coloring
of
G
is a map
\phi:V(G)\to V(H)
such that
\phi(u)\phi(v)\in E(H)
for all
uv\in E(G)
. An
H
-coloring
\phi
of
G
is
balanced
if
|\phi^{-1}(u)|=|\phi^{-1}(v)|
for any
u,v\in V(H)
, that is, color classes have the same size. Let

We prove below that if
f
is a derangement, that is if
\mathcal{S}(f)
consists of a disjoint union of cycles of length
\geq 2
, then there exists a balanced
H_{4}
-coloring of
\mathcal{S}(f)
. For inductive purpose, we prove something stronger:

Lemma 18
.

If
G
is a digraph on
4n
vertices that consists of a disjoint union of cycles, each of length
\geq 2
, then
G
has a balanced
H_{4}
-coloring.

Proof.

In this proof, for every integer
a
we set
[a]=a\mod 4
. By
coloring
we always mean
H_{4}
-coloring. We denote by
C=\{0,1,2,3\}
the set of possible colors. Given
A\subseteq C
, we say that a function
\phi:V\to C
is
A
-exceeding
if
|\phi^{-1}(a)|=|\phi^{-1}(b)|+1
for all
a\in A
and
b\in C\setminus A
; and
\phi
is
A
-defecting
if it is (
C\setminus A
)-exceeding.

Let
C_{\ell}
be a cycle of length
\ell\geq 2
with vertices
v_{0},\dots,v_{\ell-1}
in order. We say that
C_{\ell}
is of
type

t
if
t=[\ell]
. Let us prove that for any
c\in C
,

1.

if
C_{\ell}
is of type
0
then it has a balanced coloring;

2.

if
C_{\ell}
is of type
1
then it has an
\{c\}
-exceeding coloring;

3.

if
C_{\ell}
is of type
3
then it has an
\{c\}
-defecting coloring;

4.

if
C_{\ell}
is of type
2
then it has an
\{c,[c+2]\}
-exceeding coloring.

Indeed, for the type
0
, color
v_{i}
with
[i]
.
For the type
1
, color
v_{i}
with
[c+i]
for
0\leq i<\ell-5
and color
v_{\ell-5},v_{\ell-4},v_{\ell-3},v_{\ell-2},v_{\ell-1}
with
c,[c+2],c,[c+1],[c+3]
respectively.
For the type
3
, color
v_{i}
with
[c+i]
for
0\leq i<\ell-3
and color
v_{\ell-3},v_{\ell-2},v_{\ell-1}
with
[c+1],[c+2],[c+3]
respectively.
For the type
2
, color
v_{i}
with
[c+i]
for
0\leq i<\ell-2
and color
v_{\ell-2},v_{\ell-1}
with
c,[c+2]
respectively. See Figure
15
for an illustration.

We deduce that the following digraphs have a balanced coloring:

1.

a cycle of type
0
, as shown above;

2.

a disjoint union of
4
cycles of type
1
: for each
c\in C
, color one of the
4
cycles with a
\{c\}
-exceeding coloring;

3.

a disjoint union of
4
cycles of type
3
: for each
c\in C
, color one of the
4
cycles with a
\{c\}
-defecting coloring;

4.

a disjoint union of
2
cycles of type
2
: color one cycle with a
\{0,2\}
-exceeding coloring and the other one with a
\{1,3\}
-exceeding coloring;

5.

a disjoint union of
1
cycles of type
1
and
1
cycle of type
3
: color the first one with a
\{0\}
-exceeding coloring and the other one with a
\{0\}
-defecting coloring;

6.

a disjoint union of
2
cycles of type
1
and
1
cycle of type
2
: color the two first ones with a
\{0\}
-exceeding coloring and a
\{2\}
-exceeding coloring, and color the last with a
\{1,3\}
-exceeding coloring;

7.

a disjoint union of
2
cycles of type
3
and
1
cycle of type
2
: color the two first ones with a
\{0\}
-defecting coloring and a
\{2\}
-defecting coloring, and color the last with a
\{0,2\}
-exceeding coloring.

Let
G
be a non-empty digraph on
4n
vertices that consists of a disjoint union of cycles, each of length
\geq 2
.
Let us prove that
G
contains, as a subgraph, one of the digraphs listed above. Suppose, for a contradiction, that this is false. Let
a_{t}
be the number of cycles of type
t
in
G
. Since
G
does not contain the digraphs described in points
1
,
2
,
3
,
4
, we have
a_{0}=0
,
a_{1},a_{3}\leq 3
, and
a_{2}\leq 1
. Furthermore, since
G
does not contain the digraphs described in point
5
either
a_{1}=0
or
a_{3}=0
. If
a_{1}=0
(
resp.

a_{3}=0
) then all the odd cycles of
G
are of type
3
(
resp.

1
) and therefore
a_{3}
(
resp.

a_{1}
) is even (since
G
has an even number of vertices). Therefore,
(a_{1},a_{3})\in\{(0,0),(2,0),(0,2)\}
. Note that since
G
contains
4n
vertices,
[a_{1}+3a_{3}+2a_{2}]=0
. Suppose that
(a_{1},a_{3})=(0,0)
then
0=[a_{1}+2a_{2}+3a_{3}]=[2a_{2}]
and therefore
a_{2}=0
, so
G
is empty, a contradiction. Now suppose that
(a_{1},a_{3})=(2,0)
(
resp.

(a_{1},a_{3})=(0,2)
). Since
G
does not contain the digraphs described in points
6
(
resp.

7
), we have
a_{2}=0
. Therefore,
[a_{1}+2a_{2}+3a_{3}]=[a_{1}]=[2]=2
(
resp.

[a_{1}+3a_{3}+2a_{2}]=[3a_{3}]=[6]=2
) which is a contradiction. This proves that
G
contains one of the listed digraphs.

Let us now prove, by induction on the number
m
of cycles in
G
, that
G
has a balanced coloring.
If
m=1
then
G
is a cycle of type 0, which admits a balanced coloring. Suppose that
m>1
. As proved above,
G
has a subgraph
G_{1}
, with
4n^{\prime}
vertices, which admits a balanced coloring. If
G=G_{1}
we are done. Otherwise, let
G_{2}
be the subgraph of
G
obtained by deleting the cycles of
G_{1}
. Since
G_{2}
has
4(n-n^{\prime})
vertices and at most
m-1
cycles, by induction hypothesis,
G_{2}
has a balanced coloring, and with the balanced coloring of
G_{1}
we obtain a balanced coloring of
G
.
∎
