Figure 15:
Examples of coloring for the four types of cycles.

We can now prove the following strengthening of Theorem
5
.

Theorem 9
.

Let
f\in F(n)
be a derangement. There exists
h\sim f
such that, for all
x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a path from
x
to
y
of length at most
d(x,y)+4
.

Proof.

If
n=2
, then
\mathcal{S}(f)
is isomorphic to
2C_{2}
or
C_{4}
; in the first case, take
h\in F(2)
defined by
h(x)=\bar{x}
and in the second case, take
h\in F(2)
defined by
h(x)=(x_{2},\bar{x}_{1})
. So suppose that
n\geq 3
. Then,
\mathcal{S}(f)
is a digraph on
4\cdot 2^{n-2}
vertices that consists of a disjoint union of cycles of length
\geq 2
. Hence, by Lemma
18
,
\mathcal{S}(f)
has a balanced
H_{4}
-coloring
\phi
. For all
a,b\in\{0,1\}
, let
X_{ab}
be the set of
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
with
x_{1}=a
and
x_{2}=b
. Let
h=\pi\circ f\circ\pi^{-1}
where
\pi
is any permutation of
\{0,1\}^{n}
such that, for all
x\in\{0,1\}^{n}
,

•

if
\phi(x)=0
then
\pi(x)\in X_{00}
,

•

if
\phi(x)=1
then
\pi(x)\in X_{10}
,

•

if
\phi(x)=2
then
\pi(x)\in X_{11}
,

•

if
\phi(x)=3
then
\pi(x)\in X_{01}
,

•

if
\phi(x)=0
then
\pi(f(x))_{i}\neq\pi(x)_{i}
for all
3\leq i\leq n
.

The first fourth points are possible since the
4
colors classes and
\{X_{00},X_{01},X_{10},X_{11}\}
are both balanced partitions of the configurations; and the last point is possible because
f
is a derangement and the given constraints are independent with the previous ones.

Note that, for any
x\in X_{00}
,
\mathcal{A}(h)
contains the cycle of length
4
whose vertices are
x,x+e_{1},x+e_{1,2},x+e_{2}
in order. Indeed, since
x\in X_{00}
, setting
x^{\prime}=\pi^{-1}(x)
, we have
\phi(x^{\prime})=0
, so
\phi(f(x^{\prime}))\in\{1,2\}
(since
\phi
is an
H_{4}
-coloring) thus
h(x)=\pi(f(x^{\prime}))\in\{X_{10},X_{11}\}
. So
h_{1}(x)=1
and thus
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an arc from
x
to
x+e_{1}
. We prove the presence of the three other arcs of the cycle similarly.

Let
F_{4}
be the cycle of length
4
whose vertices are
00
,
10
,
01
,
11
in order, and let
d_{F_{4}}(a,b)
be the length of a shortest path from
a
to
b
in
F_{4}
. Note that,
d_{F_{4}}(a,00)+d_{F_{4}}(00,b)\leq d(a,b)+4
. Given
x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
, we denote by
\delta(x,y)
the number of
3\leq i\leq n
with
x_{i}\neq y_{i}
and set

D(x,y):=d_{F_{4}}(x_{1}x_{2},00)+d_{F_{4}}(00,y_{1}y_{2})+\delta(x,y)\leq d(x_{1}x_{2},y_{1}y_{2})+4+\delta(x,y)=d(x,y)+4.

We now prove that, for any
x,y\in\{0,1\}^{n}
,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a path from
x
to
y
of length at most
D(x,y)
. We proceed by induction on
\delta(x,y)
. The argument above shows that if
\delta(x,y)=0
then
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a path from
x
to
y
contained in a cycle of length
4
and this path is of length
d_{F_{4}}(x_{1}x_{2},y_{1}y_{2})\leq D(x,y)
. So suppose that
\delta(x,y)\geq 1
and let
3\leq i\leq n
with
x_{i}\neq y_{i}
. Let
z\in X_{00}
with
z_{j}=x_{j}
for all
3\leq j\leq n
. Since
\delta(x,z)=0
, by the same argument
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a path from
x
to
z
of length
d_{F_{4}}(x_{1}x_{2},00)
. Since
z\in X_{00}
, setting
z^{\prime}=\pi^{-1}(z)
, we have
\phi(z^{\prime})=0
and by the fifth point
h_{i}(z)=\pi(f(z^{\prime}))_{i}\neq\pi(z^{\prime})_{i}=z_{i}
. Thus,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has an arc from
z
to
z+e_{i}\in X_{00}
. Since
\delta(z+e_{i},y)=\delta(z,y)-1=\delta(x,y)-1
, by induction,
\mathcal{A}(h)
has a path from
z+e_{i}
to
y
of length at most
d_{F_{4}}(00,y_{1}y_{2})+\delta(x,y)-1
. Combining, we obtain a path from
x
to
y
of length at most
D(x,y)
.
∎

Appendix A
Theorem
8
for
n\leq 4

For
n=1
the theorem is obvious, and for
n=2
this is an easy exercise. For
n=3
, this is not difficult, but annoying, and as, moreover, one check this case easily by computer, we do not present the proof. The case
n=4
is much more difficult to check by computer but, hopefully, there is a proof almost identical to the case
n\geq 5
. Indeed, one easily check that Lemma
11
holds for
n=4
with
4
exceptions.

Lemma 19
.

Let
f\in F(4)
without fixed point. Suppose that
f^{2}\neq\mathrm{id}
and that
\mathcal{S}(f)
is not isomorphic to
\mathcal{P}_{5}+2C_{5}
,
2C_{5}+C_{6}
,
C_{4}+2C_{6}
, or
4C_{4}
. There exists
g\sim f
such that
g
properly contains a closed or
0
-open pattern
\mathcal{P}
.

Now we can prove, as in Section
5.2
, that Theorem
8
holds for
n=4
, with
4
exceptions. Indeed, let
f\in F(4)
without fixed point and suppose that
\mathcal{S}(f)
is not isomorphic to
\mathcal{P}_{5}+2C_{5}
,
2C_{5}+C_{6}
,
C_{4}+2C_{6}
, or
4C_{4}
. If
f^{2}=\mathrm{id}
then we are done by Lemma
13
. Otherwise, by Lemma
19
, there exists
g\sim f
such that
g
properly contains a closed or
0
-open pattern
\mathcal{P}
, and we are done by Lemma
12
.

It remains to treat the
4
exceptions. This is done in Figure
16
.
